newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sees 1997 deficit at 70 bln DM.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sees 1997 deficit at 70 bln DM.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday confirmed that he expected a budget deficit of around 70 billion marks ($40 billion) this year, a huge increase from previous forecasts of 53.3 billion.

But despite the surge in the deficit, Waigel said Germany would continue to strive to meet the strict fiscal targets to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and warned against talk of delaying the single currency.

"The budget deficit in 1997 will be in the range of 70 billion marks," he told members of his Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) party in Augsburg, confirming statements by government sources in Bonn.

In statements apparently aimed at his CSU rival, Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, Waigel insisted that the euro would only be launched if it were as stable as the deutschemark and dismissed talk of a postponement of monetary union.
"I can only warn against any unnecessary discussion about a delay," he said.
Stoiber has been waging a vociferous campaign to delay introduction of the euro in 1999 unless all participants strictly observe the fiscal criteria in the Maastricht Treaty.

The treaty calls for EMU particpants to meet a range of fiscal targets in 1997 to qualify for monetary union. The most important of the targets is the one that calls for EMU members to restrict budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.

The European Union's two largest members, Germany and France, both run the risk of missing the key deficit target this year. This has sparked a debate over whether monetary union should be delay if all the criteria are not met.
Waigel also seemed to be more upbeat on economic developments and said German economic growth would at least match the government's forecasts this year.
"Economic growth will be at least 2.5 percent in 1997 and between 2.7 and 2.8 percent in 1998," he said.
Waigel said the government would also present a budget for 1998 that conformed to the constitution and which envisaged a deficit lower than public investment.

The main opposition Social Democrats have filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the government, saying Waigel's budget in 1996 violated the constitutional rule that prevents the government from running a deficit above the level of public investment.
Among the many uncertainties in Waigel's budget for 1998 is financing for the planned Eurofighter military aircraft.
Waigel sought to calm fears among Germany's Eurofighter partners that the project could fail on lack of German financing.
"The Eurofighter is contained in the budget for 1998 and in the mid-term financial planning," he said.

Separately in Berlin, Manfred Bischoff, chief executive of Daimer-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA), said talks on completing financing for Germany's planned order of Eurofighter combat aircraft were going well.
Bischoff told Reuters the talks were "very constructive and positive" and he was relatively optimistic of wrapping up a deal in the next few days.
Bischoff declined to go into details of the talks, in which Waigel is seeking to claw back early around one billion marks in prefinancing granted to DASA for its Airbus civilian aircraft operations.
Closing the gap would help Germany place the 23 billion mark order for the 180 Eurofighters it wants to modernise its air force.
Germany's Eurofighter partners -- Britain, Spain and Italy -- have been concerned by the fact Bonn has not yet placed a firm order for the aircraft.
Both Waigel and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe have backed the project but have said they still need more talks to hammer out a deal on financing.
A final decision is expected to be taken by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet when they meet to agree on next year's defence budget on July 11. ($ = 1.751 German Marks)
